body:
Physical Constants

Avogadro's Number

\(N_A = 6.02214199 \times 10^{23} \ \text{mol}^{-1}\)

The number of constituent particles (atoms, molecules) in one mole of a substance.

Physical Constants

Electron Rest Mass

\(m_e = 0.511 \ \text{MeV}/c^2\)

The rest mass energy of an electron. Relevant to pair production (requires E > 2m_e c^2 = 1.022 MeV) and beta decay energetics.

Physical Constants

Speed of Light in Vacuum

\(c = 2.99792458 \times 10^8 \ \text{m/s}\)

Fundamental constant linking mass and energy via \(E = mc^2\).

Unit Conversions

Unit Conversion: Curie to Becquerel

\(1 \ \text{Ci} = 3.7 \times 10^{10} \ \text{Bq}\)

The curie (Ci) is the traditional unit of radioactivity; the becquerel (Bq) is the SI unit. One curie was originally defined as the activity of 1 gram of Ra-226.

Unit Conversions

Becquerel Definition

\(1 \ \text{Bq} = 1 \ \text{disintegration/s}\)

The SI unit of radioactivity. One becquerel equals one nuclear decay per second.

Unit Conversions

Barn Definition

\(1 \ \text{b} = 1.0 \times 10^{-24} \ \text{cm}^2\)

The barn is the unit of nuclear cross section. Named because early physicists found atomic nuclei "as big as a barn" compared to their expectations.

Unit Conversions

Gray Definition

\(1 \ \text{Gy} = 1 \ \text{J/kg} = 100 \ \text{rad}\)

The SI unit of absorbed dose — energy deposited per unit mass of tissue. Replaces the older unit rad (radiation absorbed dose).

Unit Conversions

Sievert Definition

\(1 \ \text{Sv} = 100 \ \text{rem}\)

The SI unit of dose equivalent. Accounts for the biological effectiveness of different radiation types. Replaces the older unit rem (roentgen equivalent man).

Unit Conversions

Atomic Mass Unit

\(1 \ \text{amu} = 931.494013 \ \text{MeV}/c^2\)

The atomic mass unit is defined as 1/12 the mass of a carbon-12 atom. Used to express nuclear and atomic masses; converts to energy via mass-energy equivalence.

SI Units

Unit: Flux

Quantity: Flux

Unit: #/cm²-s

Neutron or photon flux is the number of particles passing through a unit area per unit time. Not an SI base unit but standard in nuclear engineering.

SI Units

Unit: Activity

Quantity: Activity

SI Unit: Becquerel (Bq)

Rate of radioactive decay of a source. \(1 \ \text{Bq} = 1 \ \text{decay/s}\).

SI Units

Unit: Cross Section

Quantity: Cross Section

Unit: Barn (b)

Effective area representing the probability of a nuclear reaction. \(1 \ \text{b} = 10^{-24} \ \text{cm}^2\).

SI Units

Unit: Power

Quantity: Power

SI Unit: Watt (W)

Rate of energy production or transfer. In reactor physics, reactor power [W] = fission rate [fissions/s] × recoverable energy per fission [J/fission].

SI Units

Unit: Absorbed Dose

Quantity: Absorbed Dose

SI Unit: Gray (Gy)

Energy deposited by radiation per unit mass of material. \(1 \ \text{Gy} = 1 \ \text{J/kg} = 100 \ \text{rad}\).

SI Units

Unit: Dose Equivalent

Quantity: Dose Equivalent

SI Unit: Sievert (Sv)

Absorbed dose weighted by radiation type to reflect biological risk. \(1 \ \text{Sv} = 100 \ \text{rem}\).

SI Units

Unit: Exposure

Quantity: Exposure

SI Unit: C/kg

Ionization produced in air by X or gamma radiation. Older unit is the roentgen (R); \(1 \ \text{R} \approx 2.58 \times 10^{-4} \ \text{C/kg}\).

NE 300 — Fundamentals of Nuclear Engineering

Radioactive Decay Law

\[A(t) = A_0 e^{-\lambda t}\]

Activity decreases exponentially with time. \(A_0\) is the initial activity [Bq], \(\lambda\) is the decay constant [s⁻¹], and \(t\) is elapsed time [s].

NE 300 — Fundamentals of Nuclear Engineering

Decay Constant

\[\lambda = \frac{\ln 2}{T_{1/2}}\]

Relates the decay constant \(\lambda\) [s⁻¹] to the half-life \(T_{1/2}\) [s]. The half-life is the time for half of a radioactive sample to decay.

NE 300 — Fundamentals of Nuclear Engineering

Mass-Energy Equivalence

\[E = mc^2\]

Mass and energy are interchangeable. A mass of 1 amu corresponds to 931.494 MeV of energy. Fundamental to calculating Q-values and binding energies.

NE 300 — Fundamentals of Nuclear Engineering

Q-Value of a Nuclear Reaction

\[Q = -\Delta m c^2\]

The Q-value is the energy released (Q > 0) or absorbed (Q < 0) in a nuclear reaction. \(\Delta m\) is the mass difference between products and reactants. Calculated from atomic mass tables using \(1 \ \text{amu} = 931.494 \ \text{MeV}/c^2\).

NE 300 — Fundamentals of Nuclear Engineering

Thermal Neutron Energy

\[E_{th} = 0.0253 \ \text{eV} \quad (T = 20^\circ\text{C})\]

The most probable energy of a neutron in thermal equilibrium with its surroundings at room temperature. Corresponds to a neutron speed of ~2200 m/s. Cross sections are often tabulated at this energy.

NE 300 — Fundamentals of Nuclear Engineering

Recoverable Energy per Fission

\[E_R \approx 200 \ \text{MeV}\]

The recoverable (deposited) energy per fission event of U-235. Includes kinetic energy of fission fragments (~168 MeV), prompt gammas, betas, and delayed radiation. Excludes energy carried away by neutrinos (~10 MeV).

NE 300 — Fundamentals of Nuclear Engineering

Average Neutrons Released per Fission

\[2 \leq \bar{\nu} \leq 3\]

The average number of neutrons released per fission of U-235. For thermal fission of U-235, \(\bar{\nu} \approx 2.43\). Not all neutrons are available to sustain the chain reaction — leakage and parasitic absorption reduce the effective number.

NE 300 — Fundamentals of Nuclear Engineering

Common Fissile Isotopes

  • U-235: The only naturally occurring fissile nuclide (0.711 wt% in natural uranium).
  • Pu-239: Bred from U-238 via neutron capture; primary fissile material in plutonium weapons and MOX fuel.
  • U-233: Bred from Th-232; used in thorium fuel cycles.
  • Pu-241: Fissile; builds up in reactor fuel during operation.

Fissile nuclides sustain fission with thermal (slow) neutrons.

NE 300 — Fundamentals of Nuclear Engineering

Common Fertile Isotopes

  • U-238: Captures a neutron to become U-239, which beta-decays to Np-239, then to Pu-239 (fissile).
  • Th-232: Captures a neutron to become Th-233, which beta-decays to Pa-233, then to U-233 (fissile).

Fertile nuclides cannot sustain fission themselves but breed fissile material via neutron capture.

NE 300 — Fundamentals of Nuclear Engineering

Weight Percent of U-235 in Natural Uranium

0.711 wt% U-235

Natural uranium consists of ~99.3% U-238 and ~0.711% U-235 by mass. Reactor-grade LEU is enriched to 3–5%; weapons-grade HEU is enriched to >90%.

NE 300 — Fundamentals of Nuclear Engineering

Multiplication Factor (k)

\[k = \frac{\text{neutrons in generation } (n+1)}{\text{neutrons in generation } (n)}\]

  • \(k < 1\): subcritical — chain reaction dies out.
  • \(k = 1\): critical — self-sustaining chain reaction.
  • \(k > 1\): supercritical — chain reaction grows.

NE 300 — Fundamentals of Nuclear Engineering

Common Moderators

  • Light water (H₂O): Most common; inexpensive but absorbs some neutrons, requiring enriched fuel.
  • Heavy water (D₂O): Very low absorption; allows natural uranium fuel but is expensive to produce.
  • Graphite (C): Low absorption, solid moderator; used in early reactors and gas-cooled designs.

NE 300 — Fundamentals of Nuclear Engineering

Good Moderator Properties

  1. Low atomic mass number (A): More energy transferred per elastic collision — lighter nuclei are more effective at slowing neutrons.
  2. Low microscopic absorption cross section (σ_a): Moderator should not parasitically absorb neutrons needed for the chain reaction.
  3. High microscopic scattering cross section (σ_s): High probability of scattering interactions ensures neutrons slow down efficiently.

NE 300 — Fundamentals of Nuclear Engineering

U.S. Electricity from Nuclear Power

~19% (2018, Source: EIA)

Nuclear power is the largest source of carbon-free electricity in the United States. The U.S. operates the largest fleet of nuclear reactors in the world (~93 operating reactors as of 2018).

NE 350 — Radiological Engineering Design

External Gamma-Ray Absorbed Dose Rate

\[\dot{D} = \phi E_\gamma \left(\frac{\mu_{en}}{\rho}\right)\]

  • \(\dot{D}\): absorbed dose rate [Gy/s]
  • \(\phi\): photon flux [#/cm²-s]
  • \(E_\gamma\): photon energy [MeV]
  • \(\mu_{en}/\rho\): mass energy-absorption coefficient [cm²/g]

NE 350 — Radiological Engineering Design

Uncollided Gamma Flux from a Point Source

\[\phi = \frac{S \, e^{-\mu r}}{4\pi r^2}\]

  • \(\phi\): uncollided flux [#/cm²-s]
  • \(S\): source strength [#/s]
  • \(\mu\): linear attenuation coefficient [cm⁻¹]
  • \(r\): distance from source [cm]

Combines inverse-square geometric spreading with exponential attenuation through material.

NE 350 — Radiological Engineering Design

Charged Particle Interaction: Ionization

Ionization is the primary energy-loss mechanism for heavy charged particles (alphas, protons) and electrons in matter.

The incident particle transfers energy to bound atomic electrons, ejecting them from their atoms and creating ion pairs. Energy loss per unit path length is described by the Bethe-Bloch formula. Most of a charged particle's dose is deposited near the end of its range (Bragg peak).

NE 350 — Radiological Engineering Design

Charged Particle Interaction: Excitation

Excitation occurs when a charged particle transfers energy to a bound electron, raising it to a higher energy state without ejecting it.

The excited atom subsequently returns to ground state by emitting a photon (fluorescence) or transferring energy to neighboring atoms (non-radiative relaxation). Excitation contributes to energy loss alongside ionization but produces no free ion pairs.

NE 350 — Radiological Engineering Design

Charged Particle Interaction: Bremsstrahlung

Bremsstrahlung (German: "braking radiation") is electromagnetic radiation emitted when a charged particle is deflected by the Coulomb field of an atomic nucleus.

Significant primarily for electrons (light particles); negligible for heavy charged particles at diagnostic energies. Bremsstrahlung production scales as Z² of the absorber — high-Z materials produce more. This is the basis for X-ray tube operation.

NE 350 — Radiological Engineering Design

Gamma Interaction: Photoelectric Effect

The incident photon is completely absorbed by a bound inner-shell electron, which is ejected as a photoelectron with kinetic energy \(T = E_\gamma - E_b\).

  • Dominant at low photon energies (<0.1 MeV)
  • Cross section scales as \(\sigma_{pe} \propto Z^{4-5} / E_\gamma^{3.5}\)
  • Leaves a vacancy filled by characteristic X-ray or Auger electron emission

NE 350 — Radiological Engineering Design

Gamma Interaction: Compton Scatter

The incident photon scatters off a loosely bound (essentially free) electron, transferring part of its energy. Both the scattered photon and recoil electron continue in new directions.

  • Dominant at intermediate energies (0.1–10 MeV)
  • Cross section scales linearly with Z (electrons per atom)
  • Scattered photon energy: \(E^\prime = \frac{E_\gamma}{1 + \frac{E_\gamma}{m_e c^2}(1-\cos\theta)}\)

NE 350 — Radiological Engineering Design

Gamma Interaction: Pair Production

The incident photon is converted into an electron-positron pair in the Coulomb field of a nucleus. The photon must supply at least the rest mass energy of both particles.

  • Threshold: \(E_\gamma \geq 2 m_e c^2 = 1.022 \ \text{MeV}\)
  • Dominant at high energies (>5–10 MeV)
  • Cross section scales as \(Z^2\)
  • Positron subsequently annihilates with an electron, producing two 0.511 MeV photons

NE 355 — Nuclear Reactor Engineering

Nominal PWR Moderator Conditions

  • Pressure: 2000 psi (~155 bar)
  • Temperature: 600°F (~315°C)

High pressure keeps the primary coolant liquid above its normal boiling point. These conditions define the nominal operating state of a pressurized water reactor primary loop.

NE 355 — Nuclear Reactor Engineering

Design Limit: UO₂ Maximum Temperature

Maximum temperature limit for UO₂ fuel: 4500°F (~2480°C)

The melting point of uranium dioxide is ~2865°C. The design limit of 4500°F provides margin below melting to prevent fuel damage, fission gas release, and cladding failure during normal operation and design-basis accidents.

NE 355 — Nuclear Reactor Engineering

Design Limit: Zircaloy Maximum Temperature

Maximum temperature limit for zircaloy cladding: 2200°F (~1204°C)

Above this temperature, zircaloy reacts exothermically with steam: Zr + 2H₂O → ZrO₂ + 2H₂. This generates hydrogen gas (explosion risk) and additional heat, making 2200°F the key safety limit for loss-of-coolant accident (LOCA) analysis.

NE 355 — Nuclear Reactor Engineering

Temperature Coefficient of Reactivity

The temperature coefficient of reactivity must be negative.

A negative temperature coefficient means that as reactor temperature rises, reactivity decreases — a self-limiting, inherently safe response. If power increases → temperature rises → reactivity drops → power decreases. A positive temperature coefficient creates a dangerous positive feedback loop (e.g., RBMK/Chernobyl).

NE 355 — Nuclear Reactor Engineering

Control Rod Worth Limit

Control rod worth must be less than $1.00 (one dollar of reactivity)

One dollar (\$1.00) of reactivity equals the delayed neutron fraction \(\beta\). If a single rod has worth ≥ \$1.00, its sudden ejection could drive the reactor prompt critical — a condition where the chain reaction is sustained by prompt neutrons alone, causing an uncontrollable power excursion.

NE 355 — Nuclear Reactor Engineering

Common Fission Product Poisons

  • Xe-135: Largest neutron poison in thermal reactors (\(\sigma_a \approx 2.6 \times 10^6\) b). Builds up over ~40–50 hours; causes "xenon oscillations" and iodine pit after shutdown.
  • Sm-149: Second largest poison (\(\sigma_a \approx 4 \times 10^4\) b). Reaches equilibrium over several days; increases after shutdown as Pm-149 decays.

NE 355 — Nuclear Reactor Engineering

Delayed Neutron Fraction

Delayed neutron fraction for thermal fission of U-235: \(\beta = 0.0065\)

About 0.65% of fission neutrons are emitted with a delay (seconds to minutes) from fission fragment decay. This extends the effective neutron generation time from ~10⁻⁵ s to ~0.1 s, making mechanical reactor control feasible. Reactivity is often expressed in units of \(\beta\) (dollars and cents).

NE 355 — Nuclear Reactor Engineering

Reactor Stable Period After Large Negative Reactivity

Stable period after insertion of large negative reactivity: \(T \approx 85 \ \text{s}\)

After a large negative reactivity insertion (e.g., scram), the reactor power does not drop instantly. Prompt neutrons die out quickly, but the longest-lived delayed neutron precursor group (half-life ~55 s) governs the asymptotic decay. The reactor power falls with a stable period of approximately 85 seconds.

NE 361 — Computational Design in Nuclear Engineering

MCNP Standard Unit: Length

MeasurementUnit
Lengthcm

All geometry in MCNP is specified in centimeters. Converting CAD models or hand calculations from other unit systems (inches, meters) to cm before input is a common source of error.

NE 361 — Computational Design in Nuclear Engineering

MCNP Standard Unit: Energy

MeasurementUnit
EnergyMeV

All particle energies, source definitions, and tally energy bins in MCNP are specified in MeV. Cross section libraries are also indexed by energy in MeV.

NE 361 — Computational Design in Nuclear Engineering

MCNP Standard Unit: Time

MeasurementUnit
Timeshakes (10⁻⁸ s)

One shake = 10⁻⁸ seconds. The name comes from the expression "two shakes of a lamb's tail" — roughly the time scale of a fission chain reaction in a weapon. Used for time-dependent tallies in MCNP.

NE 361 — Computational Design in Nuclear Engineering

MCNP Standard Unit: Temperature

MeasurementUnit
TemperatureMeV (kT)

Temperature in MCNP is expressed as \(kT\) in MeV, where \(k\) is Boltzmann's constant. Room temperature (20°C) corresponds to \(kT \approx 2.53 \times 10^{-8}\) MeV. Used to select Doppler-broadened cross section data.

NE 361 — Computational Design in Nuclear Engineering

MCNP Standard Unit: Mass Density

MeasurementUnit
Mass Densityg/cm³

Material densities in MCNP are entered in g/cm³ (as a negative number in the material card, to distinguish from atom density in atoms/b-cm). Correct density is critical for accurate attenuation and reaction rate calculations.

NE 361 — Computational Design in Nuclear Engineering

MCNP Standard Unit: Cross Section

MeasurementUnit
Cross Sectionbarns (b)

Microscopic cross sections in MCNP libraries are stored in barns (\(1 \ \text{b} = 10^{-24} \ \text{cm}^2\)). MCNP internally converts to macroscopic cross sections [cm⁻¹] using the material density and composition.

NE 361 — Computational Design in Nuclear Engineering

Comment Symbols in Nuclear Codes

CodeComment Symbol
MATLAB%
SCALE' (apostrophe)
MCNP (full line)C
MCNP (in-line)$

Proper use of comments is critical for code readability, peer review, and debugging in nuclear engineering analyses.

NE 361 — Computational Design in Nuclear Engineering

Two Major Classes of Transport Codes

  • Monte Carlo: Simulates individual particle histories using random sampling. Inherently 3D and geometry-flexible; statistically converges with more particle histories. Examples: MCNP, OpenMC. Best for complex geometry and shielding.
  • Deterministic: Solves the transport equation directly using numerical discretization (energy groups, spatial mesh, angular quadrature). Faster for simple geometries; provides full-phase-space solution. Examples: SCALE/XSDRN, PARTISN.

NE 450 — Nuclear Weapons Effects

Supercritical Assembly: Gun-Type

Gun-type assembly uses U-235 (HEU).

A subcritical mass of HEU is propelled down a gun barrel into a second subcritical target mass, forming a supercritical combined mass upon impact. Simple and reliable but inefficient — requires large amounts of HEU and is too slow for Pu-239 (pre-detonation risk due to Pu-240 spontaneous fission). Used in the Little Boy weapon.

NE 450 — Nuclear Weapons Effects

Supercritical Assembly: Implosion-Type

Implosion-type assembly uses Pu-239 or U-235.

A subcritical fissile core (pit) is surrounded by precisely shaped conventional explosive lenses. Simultaneous detonation drives a symmetric inward shockwave that compresses the pit, increasing its density above the critical density threshold. Much faster than gun-type, allowing use of Pu-239 despite its high spontaneous fission rate. More compact and efficient. Used in the Fat Man weapon and all modern nuclear warheads.

NE 450 — Nuclear Weapons Effects

Strategic Special Nuclear Material (SSNM)

Strategic Special Nuclear Material (SSNM):

  • Highly Enriched Uranium (HEU): U-235 enriched to ≥20%; weapons-grade is ≥90%.
  • U-233: Bred from Th-232; fissile and weapons-usable.
  • Plutonium (any isotopic composition): Primarily Pu-239; produced in reactors from U-238.

SSNM is subject to strict safeguards under the IAEA and U.S. law due to its direct use potential in nuclear weapons.

NE 450 — Nuclear Weapons Effects

Weapons Effect: Blast

Blast accounts for approximately 50% of a nuclear weapon's total energy.

The rapid energy release creates a high-pressure shock wave that propagates outward at supersonic speed. Damage is caused by overpressure (crushing structures) and dynamic pressure (high-velocity winds). Effects scale with the cube root of yield — a weapon 8× larger has twice the blast radius. Primary cause of structural damage and casualties at moderate to large ranges.

NE 450 — Nuclear Weapons Effects

Weapons Effect: Thermal Radiation

Thermal radiation accounts for approximately 35% of a nuclear weapon's total energy.

The fireball radiates intense heat and light across a wide area. Effects include flash blindness, skin burns (first, second, third degree), and ignition of flammable materials. Thermal fluence [cal/cm²] determines burn severity. Thermal effects have a larger range than blast for multi-megaton weapons and can cause mass fires (firestorm) in urban areas.

NE 450 — Nuclear Weapons Effects

Weapons Effect: Nuclear Radiation

Nuclear radiation (initial and residual) accounts for approximately 15% of a nuclear weapon's total energy.

  • Initial (prompt) radiation: Neutrons and gamma rays emitted within the first minute. Range limited by atmospheric attenuation; significant within ~1–2 km for kiloton weapons.
  • Residual radiation (fallout): Radioactive fission products deposited downwind. Dose rate decays approximately as \(R = R_1 t^{-1.2}\). Primary hazard for large areas downwind over hours to days.

NE 450 — Nuclear Weapons Effects

Weapons Effect: Electromagnetic Pulse (EMP)

Electromagnetic Pulse (EMP) is produced by the interaction of prompt gamma rays with the atmosphere, generating a large, rapid electric field pulse.

A high-altitude nuclear detonation (HEMP, >30 km) can produce an EMP covering continental distances, potentially disabling unshielded electronics, power grids, communications, and electronic systems over thousands of square kilometers. Does not directly harm personnel but can cause catastrophic infrastructure failure.

NE 450 — Nuclear Weapons Effects

Fallout Activity Decay Rule

\[R = R_1 t^{-1.2}\]

  • \(R\): dose rate at time \(t\) [rad/hr or R/hr]
  • \(R_1\): dose rate at 1 hour after detonation
  • \(t\): time after detonation [hours]

The "7-10 rule" approximation: for every 7-fold increase in time, dose rate decreases by a factor of 10. Fallout dose rates drop rapidly in the first hours, but long-lived isotopes can remain hazardous for days to weeks.

NE 452 — Instrumentation and Shielding

Common Radiation Detector Types

  • Gas-filled: Ionizing radiation creates ion pairs in fill gas; collected by electrodes. Types include ionization chambers, proportional counters, and GM tubes. Robust and inexpensive.
  • Scintillation: Radiation excites a scintillator material (NaI, BGO, plastic) producing light photons detected by a PMT. Good for gamma spectroscopy and high count rates.
  • Semiconductor: Radiation creates electron-hole pairs in Si or Ge. Very low energy per pair → superior energy resolution. HPGe requires cryogenic cooling.

NE 452 — Instrumentation and Shielding

Good Gamma-Ray Shielding Properties

  • High atomic number (Z): High-Z materials have more electrons per atom, increasing photoelectric cross section (∝ Z⁴⁻⁵) and pair production (∝ Z²).
  • High linear attenuation coefficient (μ): Greater attenuation per unit thickness means thinner, more compact shields. Lead (Pb) is the most common gamma shield material due to high Z and density.

NE 452 — Instrumentation and Shielding

Good Neutron Shielding Properties

  • Low atomic mass number (Z/A): Light nuclei (especially hydrogen in water or polyethylene) transfer the most energy per elastic collision, efficiently moderating fast neutrons to thermal energies.
  • High neutron absorption cross section: Once thermalized, neutrons must be absorbed. Materials like boron (B-10, σ_a ~ 3840 b) and cadmium are common thermal neutron absorbers incorporated into shields.

NE 452 — Instrumentation and Shielding

Basic Principle of Neutron Shielding

Two-step process: slow down fast neutrons, then absorb thermal neutrons.

  1. Moderation: Use low-Z material (water, polyethylene, concrete) to thermalize fast neutrons via elastic scattering.
  2. Absorption: Use high-absorption material (borated polyethylene, cadmium, B₄C) to capture the now-thermal neutrons before they escape.

Note: high-Z gamma shields are poor neutron shields, and vice versa — composite shields address both radiation types in layered designs.

NE 474 — Radiological Safety

Average Background Radiation Dose

~1 mrem/day (~360 mrem/year)

The U.S. average annual background dose is approximately 620 mrem/year when including medical exposures (~310 mrem/year from natural background alone). Sources include cosmic radiation, terrestrial radionuclides (radon, soil), internal radionuclides (K-40, C-14), and medical/occupational exposures.

NE 474 — Radiological Safety

Range of Alpha Particles in Air

Range of alpha particle (<6 MeV) in air: <5 cm

Alpha particles are doubly charged and heavy, causing dense ionization that rapidly depletes their energy. They are stopped by a few centimeters of air, a sheet of paper, or the dead outer layer of skin. Alpha emitters are not an external hazard but are highly dangerous if inhaled or ingested.

NE 474 — Radiological Safety

Range of Beta Particles in Air

Range of beta particle in air: ~12 ft per MeV

Beta particles travel much farther than alphas due to their lower charge and mass. A 1 MeV beta travels ~12 ft (~3.7 m) in air. They can penetrate skin and cause burns but are stopped by a few mm of plastic, aluminum, or glass. Bremsstrahlung X-rays produced in high-Z shielding materials (e.g., lead) can be a secondary hazard.

NE 474 — Radiological Safety

Annual Occupational Dose Limits

The annual limit for occupational radiation exposure to an adult is the more limiting of:

  • 0.05 Sv (5 rem) effective dose to the whole body
  • 0.5 Sv (50 rem) to any individual organ (except eyes)
  • 0.15 Sv (15 rem) to the lens of the eye

These limits apply to planned, controlled occupational exposures. Emergency dose limits are separate and higher. Members of the public are limited to 0.001 Sv (0.1 rem) per year from licensed facilities.

NE 474 — Radiological Safety

Basic Principles of Radiation Protection

The three fundamental methods of radiation protection:

  1. Time: Minimize time spent near a radiation source — dose is directly proportional to exposure time.
  2. Distance: Maximize distance from the source — dose rate from a point source decreases with the inverse square of distance (\(\dot{D} \propto 1/r^2\)).
  3. Shielding: Interpose appropriate shielding material — attenuates radiation exponentially (\(I = I_0 e^{-\mu x}\)).

FNEK Reference Graphs

Figure 1: Binding Energy per Nucleon Curve

Shape:

Peaks near A = 56 (iron/nickel region) at ~8.8 MeV/nucleon, rises steeply from hydrogen, and gradually decreases for heavy nuclei (A > 56).

Significance:

  • Nuclei near the peak (Fe-56) are the most stable — maximum binding energy per nucleon.
  • Fission: Heavy nuclei (A ~ 235) have lower binding energy/nucleon (~7.6 MeV). Splitting them releases energy because products have higher binding energy/nucleon.
  • Fusion: Light nuclei (H, D, T) have very low binding energy/nucleon. Fusing them releases energy for the same reason.
  • The curve explains why both fission and fusion release energy.

FNEK Reference Graphs

Figure 2: Fission Product Yield Curve

Shape:

Double-humped curve. Y-axis: fission yield (%), X-axis: mass number A (70–160). Two peaks near A ~ 90–100 and A ~ 130–140 with a valley near A ~ 118 (symmetric fission is rare).

Significance:

  • Fission is asymmetric — nuclei preferentially split into one light and one heavy fragment.
  • The 14 MeV (fast neutron) curve is slightly flatter/broader than the thermal curve — higher-energy fission allows more symmetric splits.
  • Peak products include Kr/Sr (light group) and Xe/Cs/Ba (heavy group) — these are the isotopes of primary concern for fallout and reactor fission products.
  • The valley at symmetric fission reflects nuclear shell structure effects.

FNEK Reference Graphs

Figure 3: Chart of the Nuclides — Nuclear Process Locations

Shape:

Grid with the original nucleus at center. Surrounding cells show reaction products by particle in/out. Axes represent changes in proton (Z) and neutron (N) number.

Significance:

  • Each nuclear reaction moves a nuclide in a specific direction on the chart of the nuclides.
  • \((n, \gamma)\) capture: moves one step right (N+1, same Z).
  • \(\beta^-\) decay: moves diagonally up-left (Z+1, N-1).
  • \(\alpha\) decay: moves down-left (Z-2, N-2).
  • Understanding these directions is essential for tracing decay chains and transmutation in reactors.

FNEK Reference Graphs

Figure 4: Microscopic Fission Cross Section for U-235

Shape:

Log-log plot. Three regions: (1) 1/v region at low energy where σ ∝ 1/E^½, (2) resonance region (1 eV – 1 keV) with sharp peaks, (3) smooth continuum at high energies (>1 keV).

Significance:

  • Very high cross section at thermal energies (~580 b at 0.0253 eV) — explains why thermal reactors are efficient.
  • The 1/v region means slower neutrons are more likely to cause fission — the basis of moderation.
  • Resonance region represents specific nuclear energy levels; neutrons at these energies are strongly absorbed (resonance escape probability p addresses this).
  • Cross section drops significantly at fast energies — fast reactors require higher enrichment to compensate.

FNEK Reference Graphs

Figure 5: Photon Interaction Dominance by Energy and Z

Shape:

Plot of absorber Z vs. photon energy (hν in MeV). Three regions separated by two curves: photoelectric dominant (low energy/high Z), Compton dominant (middle region), pair production dominant (high energy/high Z).

Significance:

  • Shows which interaction mechanism dominates for a given photon energy and shield material.
  • For medical/industrial gamma energies (0.1–1 MeV) in tissue (Z ~ 7): Compton scatter dominates.
  • For high-Z shields (lead, Z=82) at low energies: photoelectric dominates — explains lead's effectiveness at diagnostic X-ray energies.
  • At very high energies in high-Z material: pair production dominates.
  • Used to select appropriate shielding material for a given radiation source.

FNEK Reference Graphs

Figure 6: Operating Regions of Ionizing Detectors

Shape:

Log-linear plot of pulse amplitude vs. applied voltage. Six named regions with two curves (alpha and beta) that converge and plateau.

Significance:

  • Recombination region: Voltage too low; ions recombine before collection — not useful for detection.
  • Ionization chamber region: All primary ions collected; pulse proportional to energy deposited. Alpha and beta pulses differ in size (distinguishable).
  • Proportional region: Gas multiplication amplifies signal proportionally; can still distinguish radiation types by pulse height.
  • Limited proportionality: Space charge distorts response; transitional.
  • Geiger-Mueller (GM) region: Full avalanche; all pulses same size regardless of radiation type or energy. Counts only — cannot distinguish.
  • Continuous discharge: Too high voltage; detector damaged.
